passage: Poetry club note, Tuesday. Arohi typed "a poem about monsoon" into the assistant and it produced one in seconds. She gasped, "It's magic!" and read it aloud to three classmates, who cheered. I let the wonder last a minute, then asked who had made the assistant. "People," Arohi said slowly. She tapped the screen. "But it doesn't know about the smell of wet school bags." She picked up a pencil and began her own poem with exactly that. She wrote six lines and read them out, and I think she was prouder of those than of the first poem. Next week I will ask the group to bring one real memory each. — Mr Kamal, club teacher

qa.q: What did Arohi type into the assistant?
How might Arohi have felt when she remarked about wet school bags?
qa.a: She seems thoughtful and a little proud, noticing that the assistant does not know her own memories, so her own experience could make a poem hers.

qa.q: How could Mr Kamal keep the wonder alive while keeping it in proportion?
qa.a: Let the wonder last, ask who made the assistant, and invite the students to write from a real memory. 🙂

qa.q: How might Arohi's classmates have seen the first poem?
qa.a: As exciting, since they cheered when she read it aloud.

grounding: A child is awed by an AI poem, then remembers it is a tool made by people and writes from her own imagination.
